nameStory: The common earthball gets its name from its round, ball-like shape and its tendency to grow right from the earth's surface, looking like nature scattered golf balls across the forest floor. The scientific name 'citrinum' means citrus-colored, referring to the yellowish tones often seen on its tough outer skin.
description: The common earthball is a round, warty fungus that looks like a small, tough ball sitting on or partially buried in the ground. Unlike true puffballs, earthballs have an extremely thick, leathery skin that feels like rough leather or pigskin when touched. They typically range from golf ball to tennis ball size and start yellowish-brown, becoming darker with age. Inside, they're filled with dark purple-black spores rather than the white flesh of edible puffballs.

idTips.label: Outer Skin
idTips.description: Thick, leathery skin that's tough to cut through, often with a warty or cracked surface pattern. Feels like rough leather and is much thicker than a true puffball's thin skin.

idTips.label: Interior
idTips.description: Dark purple-black spore mass inside, never white like edible puffballs. When mature, the interior becomes powdery and dark.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Yellowish-brown to brown exterior, sometimes with citrus-yellow tones when young. Darkens to brown or grayish-brown with age.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Often has an unpleasant, earthy or rubbery odor, especially when cut open. Some describe it as having a chemical or petroleum-like scent.

idTips.label: Attachment
idTips.description: Sits directly on the ground with no visible stem, often with root-like strands (mycelium) extending into the soil beneath.

idTips.label: Safety
idTips.description: NEVER eat earthballs - they are toxic and can cause serious illness. Always have expert identification before consuming any wild fungus.

habitat: Common earthballs grow in acidic soils under both coniferous and deciduous trees throughout New England's forests. They form partnerships with tree roots and are especially fond of sandy or well-drained soils, often appearing along woodland paths, in clearings, or at forest edges. You'll frequently find them under oaks, pines, and birches from lowland forests to mountain slopes.

seasonality.spring: Young earthballs begin forming in late spring, appearing as small, pale yellowish balls emerging from the soil. This is when they're most likely to be mistaken for edible puffballs.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for earthballs, when they reach full size and are most noticeable. The thick skin becomes more prominent and the interior spore mass darkens during hot, humid periods following rain.
seasonality.fall: Mature earthballs persist through autumn, becoming darker and more weathered. The tough skin often cracks open to release dark spores, and old specimens may look deflated or split.
seasonality.winter: Dried, empty earthball shells can persist through winter under snow, looking like dark, cracked leather balls. These remnants help identify prime locations for next year's growth.

funFact: Earthballs are nature's ultimate trick treat - they're one of the most common fungi that poison mushroom hunters mistake for edible puffballs, but their toxic compounds can cause severe digestive distress and have been used historically in some cultures as a source of yellow dye for fabrics.
confusionNotes: The most dangerous confusion is with edible puffballs, but earthballs have that distinctive thick, leathery skin you can't easily puncture with your fingernail, while true puffballs have thin, papery skin. Remember: 'Thick skin, don't begin' - if the outer layer is tough and leathery, it's an earthball and should be avoided.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'pigskin poison puffball,' earthballs aren't true puffballs at all - they belong to a completely different fungal family. This naming confusion has unfortunately led to accidental poisonings when foragers assume all round, ball-shaped fungi are safe to eat like true puffballs.
compareHints: The common earthball is typically the most abundant earthball species in New England and has the classic thick, warty skin. The many-rooted earthball has more prominent root-like attachments, while the leopard earthball has a distinctly spotted or areolated (cracked in small sections) surface pattern. Common earthballs tend to be more uniformly colored and less patterned than their relatives.
